detail.longDescription:
I saved the best for last. Or at least I thought I did. Boy was I wrong.

Regular readers know I’m more of an Apple/Mac person. I’ve used and loved Macs for decades. I stuck with Apple through the malaise era, when the company was on the brink of ruin. I don’t feel as much affection towards today’s Apple, but I still prefer iOS to Android and macOS to Windows.

In all those years, I never wrote software for an Apple platform. Now I had a convenient excuse to learn Swift and Xcode. I was feeling pretty good after my success with C# and Visual Studio, and I thought, how hard could it be?

Now that I know the answer, I somewhat regret asking the question.

When I started this leg of the journey, I didn’t realize that Swift 6 made a big deal of concurrency. Hell, I didn’t even know what concurrency was. Worse, a lot of the sample code I found was written in previous versions of Swift, so once acceptable code lit up the list of warnings like a Christmas tree. There’s also the matter of Swift being a fast-moving target. Every language evolves, every language changes, but Swift does it, uh, swiftly. There are a scary number of deprecations in Apple’s developer documentation, and that bit me in the ass countless times when repurposing existing code. The process of writing the program from start to finish felt like walking on a combination of thin ice and broken glass.

Also, if you’re considering writing a CLI program in Swift, maybe reconsider? Even though it’s possible, after what I experienced, I don’t think it should be anyone’s first choice. But if you wanna do it anyway, here’s a tip. Don’t start with an Xcode CLI PROJECT, even though it’s an option. Instead, start with a new Swift CLI PACKAGE. It’s much easier to compile for release with the latter. Xcode makes that unnecessarily difficult. Running `swift build -c release` is much, much easier.

Now I know why iOS/macOS/etc. programmers feel the need to scream on fedi periodically. Boy oh boy do I feel your pain.
